📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1284 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

According to recent reports, the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Fresh Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

Sources indicate that the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

According to recent reports, after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Recent findings suggest that start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

Industry observers note that the schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

Recent findings suggest that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table reveals that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table reveals which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Sources indicate that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In a recent development, in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Industry observers note that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

Industry observers note that the table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

In a recent development, both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() reveals which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

Brizy AI 1.9.5 Generates Website Images and Lets Customers Rework Individual Sections

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, brizy has released version 1.9.5 of its AI website builder, replacing the use of Unsplash stock photos in the AI generation workflow with generated imagery.
  • The changes give customers a way to revise part of a site without discarding a draft that already works.
  • In its version 1.9.5 announcement, Brizy states it uses components to construct a layout and can take design or content references as input.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, brizy has released version 1.9.5 of its AI website builder, replacing the use of Unsplash stock photos in the AI generation workflow with generated imagery. The revision also changes how the builder assembles pages. Brizy claims it can now generate an individual section from a prompt instead of relying on ready-made blocks for the page design.

The changes give customers a way to revise part of a site without discarding a draft that already works. They also make a distinction that matters for businesses: a stock image is an existing photograph chosen for a page, whereas a generated image can be tailored to the prompt without depicting a real product, location or member of staff. That makes some designs easier to prototype, but creates more for the site owner to verify before going live.

In its version 1.9.5 announcement, Brizy states it uses components to construct a layout and can take design or content references as input. Those references can include images or HTML for layout direction and documents for source material. An owner could start with a brand reference and then regenerate a services section when the first version misses the point, rather than regenerate every page just to change one area.

The manufacturer also says the release improves support for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian and Arabic, including right-to-left layouts for Arabic. On multilingual sites, that affects more than text. Menus, buttons and page sections must remain usable when a language runs in the other direction or when the translation takes up more space than the original. An initial generation still needs review in each language, especially on mobile.

Brizy’s separate Cloud changelog indicates that the editor and the generation flow have their own updates. For example, Cloud has added AI-assisted creation of new pages in an existing project. That is different from the new release’s ability to regenerate a single section during website creation. It is worth checking which editing surface a feature belongs to before adopting it as part of a workflow.

It has been revealed that brizy’s support guidance for WordPress import describes a generation and refinement stage before the user imports a design. It advises completing AI-based customization before the import, because the same generation controls are not available afterward in that workflow. For teams preparing a WordPress launch, that makes the handoff a good point to check copy, images and layout rather than expecting every generation option to remain available after import.

Generated imagery is useful for abstract backgrounds or illustrations when no suitable photograph exists. It is a less suitable substitute when customers need to see the actual item they are buying. Uploaded documents present a similar issue for copy: the text may look polished even if it misstates a price, service area or refund condition. Giving the builder reliable source material helps, but a person still needs to compare the published wording against it.

It has been revealed that there is also a cost to repeated experimentation. Brizy’s Cloud terms say designated AI features use credits and that consumption varies with the action. A team evaluating the update can try one representative page, revise just the section that needs work, and check how much editing remains before publication. The useful measure is not how swiftly the first design appears, but whether the site is faster to finish without losing control of what visitors see.

The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

Article: Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 20, 2026 16 min read.
  • Recent findings suggest that I almost titled this section The Failure I Should Have Expected, and honestly, that would have been the more accurate title.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover.

Nov 20, 2026 16 min read.

Recent findings suggest that I almost titled this section The Failure I Should Have Expected, and honestly, that would have been the more accurate title. The conditions were all there. I just hadn't looked at them as a system that would eventually fail, only as infrastructure that had been working fine so far. My team owned a Terraform execution platform. The registry was backed by S3, which is standard stuff. Nothing else exotic was added. One morning the dashboard lit up, showing registry failures and artifacts not downloading. We declared an incident and started the usual process of elimination.

Two hours into our investigation, I was still convinced we had done something wrong. Perhaps we had a misconfigured bucket policy or added a permissions boundary incorrectly. Hopefully, this problem was  embarrassingly fixable. I kept going back to our changes, our config, and our code. The problem wasn't in any of those places.

The actual cause took hours to surface. S3 signed URLs worked fine. You could manually call one and download an artifact without issue. But Terraform calls those URLs in sequence. When it resolves module dependencies, it fires a bunch of them back-to-back. Some of those requests were silently failing. Not all of them failed and not  in any consistent pattern, just... some, which was enough, to break the pipeline. From every dashboard we viewed, it looked like a registry bug, rather than an S3 bug.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

In a recent development, we found the real cause by building a controlled test environment on my laptop. The failures were intermittent and appeared only in production, where experimenting is discouraged, so I needed a safe way to reproduce them. I wrote a small Terraform configuration that downloads modules from our registry, the same path our pipelines use, and ran it under a load test. I also checked out the Terraform source and added logging for HTTP request and response headers. Logging exposed an easy-to-miss detail. Terraform hands module downloads to HashiCorp's go-getter library, which sends a HEAD request to each signed URL before the GET, to check whether the download can be resumed. The load test reproduced the failure within ten minutes; the logs traced it to that HEAD request rather than to our registry. I proposed that a recent change in how AWS handled the HEAD request was producing the downstream 404.

Sources indicate that this hypothesis was initially not obvious even to their support personnel. I substantiated it with clear reproduction steps and diagnostic evidence. After they escalated internally to their architecture team, they confirmed that a recent change in request handling was the root cause and rolled back the change, restoring expected behavior. The lesson I took from this situation was when a managed dependency fails intermittently, reproduce your client's exact call pattern outside of production and instrument the client, not just the server.

According to recent reports, detection took a few hours. Recovery took nearly twenty-four hours, most of which was spent on support calls proving the issue was on their end waiting for AWS to acknowledge other customers were affected and waiting for the rollback to ship. Once AWS rolled back the S3 deployment, concurrent signed URL requests stabilized and the registry recovered without any changes on our end.

According to recent reports, the mechanism here, signed URLs, concurrency, isn't the important part. The important part is the assumption I had been running on without examining it, that cloud infrastructure is reliable by default. That 99.99 percent is essentially "always works". I had treated the SLA like a guarantee rather than a statistical claim about a distribution with a tail I just hadn't seen yet.

Fifty-two minutes and thirty-six seconds of downtime per year. Considering the scale at which we were operating, hitting that window was not a matter of if, because I already had and more than once. I just hadn't treated it as evidence that my design needed to change.

Sources indicate that every organization I have worked for has made the same mistake and I bet that yours has too. Someone builds an observability system early on. They care about it. The dashboards are thoughtful, the alerts are calibrated, and the runbooks are linked. Then the system grows, engineers move on, haphazardly adding and wiring  in latest services without anyone updating what came before. The people who built the original dashboards aren't around to update them and the people who are around are nervous to touch something they didn't build and don't fully understand. Alerts drift out of calibration and dashboards start showing concerns nobody on the current team knows how to interpret.

Industry observers note that then something breaks at a bad hour and the person on call opens Grafana and spends twenty minutes just trying to figure out what they are seeing. I have been in that position. The problem runs deeper than knowledge. It is a design failure, not a skills gap. The dashboards were built as a reporting layer, something that reveals you what is happening. But they were never connected to anything that does something about what is happening. The human is still the bridge between signal and response.

Recent findings suggest that the mistake has nothing to do with tooling choice, query language, or dashboard layout. The mistake is treating observability as a way to inform humans rather than a way to drive system behavior. The difference is significant in practice. In reporting, a human receives an alert, interprets it under stress at a bad hour, decides what to do, and acts. In a control plane, the system receives and evaluates the signal against a defined policy, acts, and tells the human what happened. One of those scales with your headcount and on-call rotation, while the other breaks the moment both are stretched thin.

Sources indicate that none of the tooling required for this design is upcoming. Prometheus has had alerting rules and webhook routing for years. Terraform can reconfigure routing weights. The components all exist; they just haven't been wired together with automation as the explicit goal. The pattern is the same at every scale, from pod autoscaling to regional failover: observe, decide, act, and confirm.

I have run Prometheus and Grafana stacks across hundreds of services, large builds and deployment pipelines, with thousands of executions per day. These tools are powerful but carry an operational cost teams consistently underestimate. Consider that expertise concentrates. When the person who really knows the stack leaves, calibration drifts silently until something breaks at the worst possible moment. Treat your observability stack with the same ownership model as your production services with regular reviews, real failure testing, and collective ownership that does not expire when the original author leaves.

Figure 1. Observability as a reporting layer vs. a control plane.The difference is whether a human or the system bridges signal to response. (Source: created by author.).

I have never worked with anyone who needed a whitepaper to understand why multi-region matters. Instead, they needed an outage. After a major regional failure hit one of our cloud providers, the conversation about moving the Terraform registry to active-active architecture happened. The registry is called during every pipeline execution: every build, every deployment, and every release. When it goes down, every build, every deployment, and every release across every team stops with it. The blast radius of that dependency is much larger than it looks on an architecture diagram; it took a real outage for that to land viscerally for everyone involved.

In a recent development, we chose active-active, not active-passive. The reason for this choice comes up less often in architecture discussions than it should. We wanted the secondary region under real production load before we needed it for failover.

Recent findings suggest that active-passive looks good in diagrams. The failure mode is subtle and tends to surface at the worst possible time. The passive region has never handled your actual traffic. Its configuration has drifted unnoticed. Caches are cold and downstream dependencies haven't been exercised under anything close to real load. You have tested it in staging, maybe, with synthetic load that doesn't match your real traffic profile. When you fail under pressure, during an active incident with people watching, you discover all of these issues simultaneously.

Industry observers note that I have been on that incident bridge. It is a specific kind of unpleasantry. You are trying to recover from one problem while discovering a second set of problems you didn't know you had. Active-active costs more. You have to keep regions in sync. Data consistency under partition requires careful thought. But when a region degrades, you shift load in a system that has been running in two regions all along, not making a leap of faith into an untested environment. We ran 50/50 under normal operation, which gave us continuous validation. Both regions were exercised constantly under real load. But 50/50 is the steady state, not the failure state. When a region actually degrades, traffic shifts to 100/0.

According to recent reports, that transition is what you are building toward and it has to be tested deliberately. We ran chaos testing specifically for this situation. Cut one region entirely, verify the other absorbs full load cleanly, and confirm recovery when it comes back. If you haven't tested the 100/0 state, you haven't tested your disaster recovery (DR) system. Instead, you have tested your routing config. Multi-region is expensive to build and maintain. For a critical build-time dependency like this registry, it was the right call. But it should be a deliberate decision, not a default assumption.

Two failure modes in this design are worth being honest about, because neither shows up in a clean chaos test. The first is a failure that is not regional at all. The S3 incident hit both regions at the same time, because both depended on the same S3 behavior. Regional failover cannot fix that problem. Failover shifts traffic to the other region, which is failing the same way, so failover triggers there too and traffic shifts back. The automation keeps moving traffic between two broken regions and adds noise to an incident it cannot resolve. Route 53 behaves the same way at the DNS layer. When every weighted record is unhealthy, it returns all of them rather than none. When both regions degrade together, the cause is a shared dependency. The correct automated response is to hold traffic where it is and page a human.

The second failure mode is a health check that reports the wrong thing. Our /health endpoint confirmed that the application process was running, not that it could do its job. If the backend database in one region goes down, the application keeps answering /health with 200 OK while real requests fail. This is exactly the case for which regional failover exists, but Route 53 sees a healthy endpoint and keeps sending traffic to the broken region. The confirmation Lambda checks the same endpoint, so it would also report a failover into that region as successful. A health check has to exercise the functionality the service delivers, such as a lightweight database read, not just confirm the process is up. Deep checks carry their own risk. If the dependency they test is shared by both regions, they bring back the first failure mode.

Sources indicate that DNS TTL is the single most common DR misconfiguration I have seen in otherwise well-designed systems and it is worth addressing directly. TTL controls how long a resolver caches a DNS record before requerying. If the setting is too high (e.g.,  three hundred seconds, six hundred seconds, or whatever the module default happened to be) and your failover logic can fire correctly, then your routing weights can enhancement correctly and clients will keep hitting the degraded region for minutes because their resolvers haven't expired the old record. The failover executed correctly, but the traffic never moved because resolvers were still serving the cached record.

In a recent development, if the setting is too low, then you have built an overreactive system. A transient latency spike triggers a DNS change. The issue resolves thirty seconds later. Now you have regions flip-flopping and amplifying instability that would have cleared on their own. The right TTL is a deliberate number, chosen against your RTO, your health check interval, and your false positive tolerance. Most teams are running whatever default Infrastructure as code (IaC) module was set years ago. They don't know what that number is until they are debugging a failover that didn't go the way they expected.

Sources indicate that figure 2. DNS TTL and failover timing. A weight change that fires correctly can still leave traffic stranded in the degraded region until resolver caches expire. (Source: created by author.).

What separates DR systems that actually work from those existing only on paper is automation with confirmation, not just detecting failure, but acting on it and verifying the action succeeded. Most teams that have invested seriously in DR have detection, such as alerts that fire when error rates spike or health checks fail. Fewer have built the response layer, the automated action that runs when the signal fires. Fewer still have built the confirmation layer, the part checking whether or not the response actually worked.

This last piece matters more than people realize. Automated failover without confirmation is a system taking an action and then going quiet. Did the secondary region receive the traffic? Did DNS propagate before the TTL window? Are the downstream dependencies there responding correctly? A system capable of answering these questions by continuing to observe after acting is one you can trust. A system that only fires and then goes silent is an untested hypothesis.

Recent findings suggest that the pattern looks like this in practice: A Prometheus alerting rule evaluates a composite signal, error rate above threshold AND p99 latency elevated AND sustained for a defined window. This observation is crucial. Single-metric alerts are noisy. A transient spike fires them constantly for things that resolve on their own in a minute or two. The composite condition with a duration requirement indicates you only trigger degradation that has actually persisted.

Most implementations stop at the alert. Here the alert is the entry point to an automated chain. How traffic moves depends on the topology. In an active-active setup, Route 53 does the switching. Each regional record carries a weight and a health check. When a region's health check fails, Route 53 stops returning that record, so traffic shifts to the healthy region with no custom code. In an active-passive setup, the alert drives the switch. Alertmanager routes it to a webhook, which invokes a Lambda function that flips the Route 53 failover record to the secondary region. In both cases, the alert also triggers a confirmation Lambda that polls the target region's health endpoint until it confirms the region is returning healthy responses. The human receives a notification only after the Lambda confirms the loop completed successfully. Detection, action, and confirmation form one connected loop. Observability drives the action and then verifies the outcome.

Figure 3. The detect–act–confirm loop. Prometheus fires, Route 53 shifts traffic, Lambda polls until the target region confirms healthy, then notifies the team. (Source: created by author.).

That confirmation loop, in practice, looks like this:.

According to recent reports, the loop does not close until the health check returns 200. If it never does, the function returns unconfirmed and that signal itself becomes an alert, not a silent failure.

According to recent reports, this is a Terraform configuration for the Route 53 side. Both regions carry equal weight and Route 53 stops returning a region's record when its health check fails:.

Sources indicate that the by (region) clause is what makes this rule region-aware. It evaluates the composite signal independently per region, so when one region degrades while the other remains healthy, the alert fires with the specific region label that tells the automation exactly which region is degraded.

According to recent reports, the for: 90s is doing real work there. Without it, this alert fires on blips. With it, the alert fires only when something has been consistently degraded for a minute and a half, which is a meaningfully different situation.

Finally, there is testing. The most effective practice I know for thorough testing is the game day,  a scheduled exercise where the team deliberately injects real failures into production systems and works through detection, response, and recovery in real time, with the people who would handle a real incident in the room. It is not a runbook walk-through in staging.

Game days find the human gaps as reliably as they find technical ones. Who actually has decision authority when you cannot reach the incident commander? Where is the runbook for this failure mode, exactly? Does everyone know? The first time most teams run one, the answer to these questions is uncomfortable. That is the point. Finding it during a game day costs an afternoon.

The validation that teams most consistently skip is testing that the confirmation layer correctly recognizes a successful failover and stops taking action. People test that the failover fires. They rarely test what happens if it fires and the system thinks it didn't work. That is a real path to cascading failures you created yourself.

The S3 incident wasn't something I had modeled. Nobody had a runbook for "S3 silently breaks concurrent signed URL requests under load following an internal deployment". The assumption that underpins a lot of how we build systems, that the infrastructure below us is basically reliable, is fine most of the time, which is exactly why it is so rarely questioned.

Three steps will turn your failover proposal into a working system. First, pick one alert that pages a human today and wire it to an automated response with a confirmation step. Second, put your secondary region under real production traffic before you need it for failover. Third, on your next game day, test the confirmation layer, not just the trigger. Verify that the system recognizes a successful failover and stops acting. If you haven't validated all three, you have a plan, not a system.

Infrastructure will fail, and the next failure will probably be one you haven't seen before. Whether a person has to piece together a response manually or the system handles it was decided long before the incident started.

Breaking: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • It has been revealed that in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • Recent findings suggest that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

It has been revealed that in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

Recent findings suggest that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

According to recent reports, the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

It has been revealed that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

Industry observers note that the second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

According to recent reports, this effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping organization that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

Recent findings suggest that the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Sources indicate that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a fresh idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

According to recent reports, first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping organization: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

In a recent development, third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

It has been revealed that the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

According to recent reports, the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

Industry observers note that to find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

In a recent development, vocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

In a recent development, vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Sources indicate that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Companies are giving AI a bigger role in decisions, but that does not mean their leaders find decisions easier. In a survey published by Körber, 76% of senior decision-makers noted decision-making had become more complex. The same share reported allowing AI to play a greater role. The answers describe two trends happening at the same time; they do not establish that one caused the other.

The survey included 2,000 senior executives, split evenly between the United States and Germany. Körber says respondents worked for organizations with annual revenue above $250 million and at least 250 employees, and fieldwork ran from August 27 to September 8, 2026. That makes the findings a look at decision-making inside larger organizations in two markets, not a representative measure of every employer or of small businesses.

According to recent reports, the accompanying release states 74% of respondents reported that information volume can get in the way of decisions, while 75% said decisions stall when critical information is not available at the right time. Having more data and having the right data when a decision is due are different problems.

According to recent reports, consider a manager who needs to decide whether to delay a shipment. Sales, warehouse operations and finance may have different records for the same order, all updated at different times. An AI assistant can summarize those records swiftly, but a faster summary does not establish which number is current or who can approve an exception. Unless the team can check the sources and resolve conflicting records, the tool can move the work of reconciliation from one person to another rather than eliminate it.

Industry observers note that the survey also found that 73% of respondents were uncomfortable letting technology make the final decision. That helps explain why businesses may want AI in the workflow without giving it control of the outcome. Drafting an explanation, gathering supporting documents and making a decision that commits the company are separate jobs. The cost of an error differs for each.

Among respondents whose organizations described their transformation as enterprise-wide, 63.8% reported strong organizational performance, compared with 41.6% of those at the pilot stage. Future-readiness confidence was 66.4% and 46.5%, respectively. Prepares to invest significantly in AI decision support were almost identical: 59% for the enterprise-wide group, versus 59.4% for the pilot group.

In a recent development, those are self-reported group differences, not measured returns from a controlled rollout. Organizations that can implement technology across departments may already have stronger data, more resources or better operating processes. The publication does not establish that expanding a pilot causes performance to improve. It is better read as a prompt to ask what mature implementations do differently and which of those practices a particular team can test.

In a recent development, the practical question for an operator is where a tool improves the work between a question and a decision. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a way to formalize responsibilities and decide what to measure in context. Teams can pick a recurring decision and compare how long it takes to obtain the necessary evidence, how often a recommendation must be corrected and whether an approver can explain what they relied on.

Tracking these measures separately can reveal a trade-off that a single adoption number misses. A tool may produce reports faster while increasing the time spent checking them, or it may let people spend less time gathering facts and more time evaluating options. For the executives surveyed, the challenge is not simply making AI more available. It is defining the role it plays when information is incomplete and someone still has to own the decision.

Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done.
  • It has been revealed that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

It has been revealed that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Sources indicate that figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Recent findings suggest that each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Sources indicate that then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

It has been revealed that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

In a recent development, what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but organization policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

Sources indicate that thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly latest solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

Industry observers note that and bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

In a recent development, the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Sources indicate that average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

According to recent reports, the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Industry observers note that pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

According to recent reports, figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

Recent findings suggest that the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

Recent findings suggest that the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Sources indicate that training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

It has been revealed that for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each enhancement generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

In a recent development, no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

Recent findings suggest that thinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

It has been revealed that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

Sources indicate that the question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

It has been revealed that so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

In a recent development, each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

According to recent reports, figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

According to recent reports, we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Recent findings suggest that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO enhancement.

It has been revealed that figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

According to recent reports, when sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

It has been revealed that when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

Recent findings suggest that in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that databricks has added PostgreSQL 19 to Lakebase and Neon, giving teams a way to try the open-source database’s new maintenance, query planning and replication tools on managed infrastructure. Databricks says both services had support on the day the PostgreSQL project released the new version. PostgreSQL’s own announcement dates the community release to November 19, 2026.

It has been revealed that the update is relevant to teams building AI applications, even though it does not introduce a new AI model or vector index. Operational databases often sit behind the user-facing parts of these systems. They store conversation history, track jobs and permissions, record application events and serve calls that need predictable response times. A database upgrade that makes this infrastructure easier to maintain can matter more to those teams than a new feature in the application layer.

According to recent reports, one of the main additions in the PostgreSQL 19 release is REPACK, a command that rebuilds a table to reclaim unused space and can optionally reorder the data to match an index. PostgreSQL creates a newly introduced row version when data changes. Routine vacuuming makes old space available for reuse, but that does not always shrink the underlying table on disk. A table that stores frequently updated jobs or messages can keep occupying more space than its remaining live rows need.

An option lets ordinary reads and writes continue through most of the rebuild. That does not make the operation free of disruption. As Neon’s release notes explain, PostgreSQL still needs an exclusive lock to finish swapping the rebuilt files into place. Teams should test the operation under a representative write load rather than assume the final lock is negligible on a busy table.

It has been revealed that the release also adds pg_plan_advice, an extension for testing and stabilizing execution plans, and a companion pg_stash_advice extension that can apply stored advice to a matching query. The planner ordinarily chooses how to execute a query based on the data and statistics available. When that choice changes, an operation that used to be fast can suddenly become slow. The latest tools give operators a way to investigate or mitigate that regression without immediately rewriting application code. Any saved advice should be revisited as the data and workload evolve.

PostgreSQL 19 also adds WAIT FOR LSN, which lets an application wait for a database replica to reach a specified position in the write-ahead log. With asynchronous replication, a write can succeed on the primary database before a replica has applied it. A user or agent that immediately reads from that replica may otherwise see an earlier state.

That lag matters if, for example, an application records approval for a task and immediately asks another service to read it from a replica. Waiting for the relevant log position can let that read see the approval. It trades some waiting time for freshness when the workflow needs it, rather than assuming all replica reads are current.

According to recent reports, databricks’ supported-versions documentation lists PostgreSQL 19 for Lakebase, and Neon’s announcement explains how to choose it for a fresh project. Neither announcement claims that all existing databases were automatically upgraded. Databricks also says Lakebase engineers contributed to the upstream release, including work on query-strategy advice, shared memory and release management.

In a recent development, for teams considering a migration, version availability is a starting point. A useful test is to run representative queries, confirm extension compatibility, measure replica lag and rehearse the maintenance operations that prompted the upgrade. Teams can then compare those results with the behavior of their current database before switching production traffic.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: The Future of Apache Iceberg.
  • Nov 20, 2026 3 min read.
  • Sources indicate that apache Iceberg V4 proposes a redesign of table metadata to improve scalability and support more frequent writes, alongside new capabilities for data management and schema evolution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: The Future of Apache Iceberg.

Nov 20, 2026 3 min read.

Sources indicate that apache Iceberg V4 proposes a redesign of table metadata to improve scalability and support more frequent writes, alongside new capabilities for data management and schema evolution. Daniel Weeks, co-creator of Apache Iceberg and member of technical staff at Databricks, presented a session at QCon San Francisco on the fourth version of the Apache Iceberg open table format specification.

Iceberg V4 will address the limitations of managing very large tables while expanding the format to support new data types and workloads. The speaker described the new version as a major reimagining of the table format rather than an incremental step, with changes including a new metadata tree, more efficient commits, typed column statistics, relative file paths, and support for file and vector data types. While earlier versions left most of the metadata structure intact, V4 addresses problems that emerge at large scale and adds support for new use cases. Weeks told the audience in San Francisco:.

V4 is a major reimagining of a table format. We didn't get everything right in V3 and prior, so now we're taking the opportunity to fix some of the biggest things that are challenges as we scale up to even larger data sets and we bring on latest use cases.

Apache Iceberg is an open table format for managing large analytical datasets across different data processing engines. Originally developed at Netflix in 2017, it was open-sourced in 2018 and became an Apache top-level project in 2020. The main alternatives among open table formats are Delta Lake, created by Databricks and now a Linux Foundation project, Apache Hudi, originally developed at Uber, and Apache Paimon, which grew out of the Flink community and gained adoption for streaming-oriented workloads. However, interoperability tools are increasingly blurring the lines between them.

In his talk, Weeks covered three areas of the proposed Iceberg V4 changes: metadata and scalability, including the Adaptive Metadata Tree, single-file commits, improved column statistics, relative paths, and column-level updates; latest table features, such as expression-based default values and constraints; and new data types, particularly file and vector types, which support additional workloads such as AI and search. Regarding faster commits, Weeks explained:.

This gets us into use cases where we can stream data much faster. We can do commits at the 2nd level or subsecond level, where right now we largely recommend that you don't do commits under 2 minutes.

In a recent development, in V3, adding a data file requires at least four I/O operations, including manifest creation and rewriting. V4 simplifies this process by allowing the metadata tree's root to point directly to data files, reducing the operation to a single metadata write. According to Weeks, this could enable commits every second or even at subsecond intervals, compared with the current recommendation of at least two minutes between commits. Iceberg V3, introduced in 2024, added deletion vectors, row lineage, new data types, encryption, and default values.

According to recent reports, V4 replaces V3's binary column statistics with structured, typed statistics, improving projection and schema evolution. Furthermore, V4 introduces expression-based default values, check, unique, and primary key constraints, and statistics-only fields that support partitioning, sorting, and filtering without storing additional data. It will also track constraint validation status, allowing engines to determine when further checks are needed.

In August, Weeks started an initial V4 scope discussion on the Apache Iceberg developer mailing list, with Steven Wu suggesting adding monotonic snapshot and row-level patch timestamps, while Manu Zhang discussed efficient column updates and the removal of equality deletes.

Industry observers note that during the Q&A, Weeks explicitly confirmed that V4 metadata will not be backward compatible with older readers. Existing V3 metadata can remain in place during an upgrade, but older readers cannot consume the new representation.
