InfoQ Homepage Presentations Modernising Retail at Scale: Architecting a Cloud‑to‑Edge Platform for a Global Enterprise.

Industry observers note that jayesh Bhayani discusses Tesco’s decade-long enterprise transformation from fragmented legacy systems to a unified cloud-edge platform. He explains how aligning system, talent, and process modernizations allowed Tesco to scale mission-critical retail operations to millions of customers, while sharing practical lessons on build vs. buy, cloud cost management, and preparing for agentic commerce.

Jayesh Bhayani is Senior Engineering Director at Tesco, playing a central role in leading technology strategy and shaping business direction. His work focuses on creating strategic clarity, architectural direction, and organizational alignment needed for the business to compete at pace in an increasingly disruptive retail environment, driving enterprise scale and agentic commerce readiness.

Software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Recent findings suggest that jayesh Bhayani: I'm going to spend some time in sharing our learnings of transformation at scale at Tesco. That's why modernizing technology at Tesco. How it has changed the culture, not just within the company, along with systems, but enabled the growth for the company. From that perspective, after 10 years being at Tesco, I thought it would be good to share the learnings we had from here and how we are looking at the future.

I was in California, in Silicon Valley, for about 25 years, when Tesco reached out to me, saying, would you like to work at Tesco? I had got no concept of Tesco, because I had never come to London before that. When I looked at the website, it was a pretty basic website. The outside-in perspective, when you look at the website of a large grocery chain, feels like there is no technology. This went on for a few months. After that, they convinced me to talk to a few people in the technology department. The state that this technology was, and what was needed for growth and the transformation that was needed at scale, was what motivated me and my wife. We were empty nesters already by that time. We decided, why not? Came here. Just around that time, Trump got elected. We felt even better.

Industry observers note that first of all, some context into how large Tesco is. There are about 5,000 stores. Some of them are super. Some of them are medium. Some of them are small. They are across five different countries. We used to be in Asia as well, when I started 10 years back, in Thailand, Malaysia. We divested those businesses. We are still in five countries. We have 20 distribution centers. We have 25 million customers. That's almost one-third of the UK population. That's not small. We have 350,000 colleagues across our stores. Out of that, maybe around 15,000 in head office. Out of that, around 6,000 in technology. Again, it's substantial. It's big operations, large number of colleagues. We do around 50 million baskets. Not number of transactions, the baskets, which means the orders across our estate in our stores. We do 1.3 million online orders in a week. When COVID came, many companies talk about scale.

When COVID happened, when entire business shifted towards online, our challenge was to double the number of online slots that we can make available for our customers. By that time, for the e-commerce part, our platform was already live. When we doubled it, that's equivalent of putting almost three other competitor companies online in one month. Many companies stopped taking orders. Many companies stopped signing customers. We doubled it in a month. That again indicates the scale. Fifty million cases through supply chain, huge. We are not even talking about number of miles the trucks travel and the logistics within the distribution center. We do 4.5 billion calls a day. We have 98% UK coverage when I talk about 25 million customers, but coverage-wise in terms of online business, that can cover the entire geography of UK. We cover almost 98%, which means you can have your home delivery of grocery done in 98% of the UK.

Tills, as we call it here in the UK, POS systems, as called in many other countries, almost 50,000. That's just POS devices. We are not talking about all other thousands and tens of thousands of handheld devices that run on the same platform. That's just the context, because that sets a very different tone for the kind of technology, how mission-critical technology becomes. Then driving transformation through that is quite challenging, because I worked at startups. I've worked at mid-size companies. I had my own startup. Being in California and not having a startup is a crime. I tried that, too. I worked at Yahoo for 10 years. I worked at large companies, worked at startups. Tesco is yet another scale. I wanted to reflect here, because it drives quite a lot of complexities in decision-making of what would you do with your transformation and technology choices.

Recent findings suggest that this goes beyond retail. Any industry that has got physical estate, digital, and real-time operations will face these complexities. That's where we learned about being both efficient and effective. Efficient is do things well, fast. Effective, do good things, which are more effective. A slight difference in nuances. You can be doing fast all the things, but if those are not the right things, you are chasing wrong goals. Do the right things and do things the right way, efficiency and effectiveness. I wanted to share here, this is not just about retail. This will apply to many of the industries who operate at that kind of scale and complexity.

According to recent reports, let's start as to why. Ten years back, why did we need transformation? It was quite a poor state within technology I'm talking. When they talked about a large grocery firm and I was thinking there is no technology inside, there was a lot of technology, but it was very siloed. Multiple technology stacks tied to historical business structures. When I'm talking siloed, this is not just, store had a POS system and e-commerce had something else. I'm talking multiple stacks within online or e-commerce business itself. Grocery, its entire stack. We had marketplace back then, completely different stack. One Microsoft, .NET, one Oracle. F&F, our clothing, Tesco wine. Customers across these, forget having single account, did not even have single login. Jayesh@groceryhomeshopping is different than Jayesh@marketplace, is different than Jayesh@f&f. We had no single customer view, no data platforms, no product management, nothing. It was that fragmented. There was no single identity, as I just explained.

Recent findings suggest that no single source of truth for stock or pricing. From that perspective, when you have multiple monolithic systems running in private data centers, we were not in public cloud back then. It was not even private data cloud. It was just a bunch of machines. You would be lucky if you asked for a server and you get a server in two months. That was the state. Decades old POS system, 20 years old software running on our POS systems in the stores, completely batch oriented. You couldn't connect to them. The deployments were the engineers would go with the floppy disk and then will deploy the software in the stores. Third-party solutions, not just third-party solutions, they were heavily customized, because when you are at the scale of Tesco, you can demand saying, I need a slightly different thing in your software. Sounds good initially. Then you're locked in with a very customized version of vendor solution for multiple years.

According to recent reports, we had software running from vendor solutions that were at least a decade old. You can't even upgrade them. Then heavily outsourced resources as well. These were where we had lots of consulting firms providing resources for us. Not a good culture, not good quality. You can imagine what the landscape was when we started 10 years back. At the scale of Tesco, that becomes quite complex to say, how do you find your journey through that?

Recent findings suggest that that got us the imperative for change, saying we definitely need omnichannel experience, because customer expectations were moving very fast. The old style of doing business was not working. Technology was not helping business. Business had all the motivation to change. Technology was stuck. We had hit the wall, literally. Global coherence across physical and digital estate, both. Rapid change cycles. Back then, as I said, if you talked to a vendor and asked for a solution in our POS systems, it would be six months for minor changes. Regression on top of that, so three things would be broken. You do the testing, and they charge you for fixing the bugs again. It would be six to nine months before you could get anything out on our Tills or POS systems in stores. Forget e-commerce. Then along with that, of course, we needed higher reliability, higher capability. We needed omnichannel experience, higher security, everything.

It needed more capability and capacity, both. That led to us chasing from fragmented stacks to unified platforms that could serve all our channels across all our markets and develop a multi-tenant platform. That's what we developed. It was called only platform. Sometimes platform terms are confusing. I'm not talking just the tech platform. I'm talking about the retail platform that runs our business. We'll talk about tech platform as well. That's part of our learning as to how tech platforms are super important if you don't start early. When we started, it was a retail platform to say, how do we now enable all these businesses and develop the retail platform?

Where are we now? All of our entire UK business and Republic of Ireland business runs on this platform, 100%. We are making inroads in our Central European businesses. There are multiple countries there. They all have their nuances. The trust in technology is much higher. Technology strategy is very well integrated with the business strategy. It's not like service-oriented mindset of say, we just need three things. Go ahead and can you build it? That's how the siloed happened long time back. We'll talk about that in our transformation journey. As I remarked, the platform is much more scalable but also capable. That's where we are now. We'll talk about how we are looking into the future of agentic commerce from that perspective. Technology has become an integral part of the entire business ecosystem. It's no longer a separate unit that sits in a corner and gets three orders to say, can you develop this for us?

This I describe in my own language. Let's now talk about the journey of transformation. Most companies most people assume that when you talk about transformation, you're talking about system transformation, which is, develop the platforms. We'll talk more about that. That's what I talked about until now. That's not enough. What we had to do along with that was talent transformation. Was very service-oriented mindset, as I mentioned. Most of the development was outsourced. We had to completely change our career paths, the titles within that, the job definitions within that, and completely transform the talent internally. When you want to insource that, that's a huge task. Back then we were only across two different locations, UK and India. As part of this transformation, we started two more, Hungary and Poland, because we had to scale and we needed good talent. The combination of that was required. As I said, the career frameworks were redefined across product, engineering, and program.

According to recent reports, product did not exist. Product management did not exist back then. It was only program and mostly service engineering. The right org structure is super notable as part of that as well. You can have talent, but if they're not set up in the right organization, it does not work. It generally should map the business domains and the business structure. For example, in Tesco, there are four major business units, supply chain and distribution, commercial unit where you decide as to, should we sell potatoes and tomatoes that leads to almost a ranging of 40,000, 100,000 SKUs saying what are we going to sell across our estate? What should be the price of that? What should be the cost of that? What kind of promotion should we run? What kind of store design should be there? How many aisles should be there? Which product goes in which aisle? That's completely very complex business.

Recent findings suggest that that's all trading decisions. Channels, which is where online and stores where customers actually buy things. Then customer area, which is mostly loyalty programs and stuff like that. We had to mimic that within technology to say we are going to completely map ourselves into how the company is laid out. You can't run your own ship in a large company and say that we are just different. That doesn't work. Because if you're not sustainable, transformation will not work. That's talent transformation, and we had to change recruitment processes well along with that. The third pillar of this one was process transformation. You can have the right talent, you have the right motivation because you need good challenges for right talent, which is system transformation. If your processes are not conducive, then that fails. The reason why we had silos, not that anything is wrong with program management. We still have hundreds of program managers, but the role of program manager was very different.

In a recent development, some business person would have a favorite person in technology, as I said, it was a phone call away. No one knew about technology. They will talk to a program person and say, can you get this done? They will run around, talk to a bunch of service engineers, outsource it, comes back a solution. The silo gets deeper and deeper and deeper. We had to establish that from program led, we are going to be an agile product-driven firm. We develop products, not just solutions. We'll talk more about some of these, mostly in the systems area. I'll refer to a couple other things as needed, because today is just a teaser of the transformation. I'm trying to compress 10 years of our learnings.

That led to, in the system transformation, what's the strategic framework? One of the very early things we had to decide was build and buy. Build versus buy, many people call it, we call it build and buy. Why? Because while we wanted to insource and build the platform internally with insource resources, you will need to buy many technologies along with that. What we stated was, we'll always tend towards building things which are core differentiator for our business. That's how we will win. Something that is not a core differentiator, we'll just buy. Most of the enabling function, as we call it internally, which is back-office applications like people system, finance system, everything, they're not a core differentiator. The retail platform is a core differentiator, including the POS system that runs on every single Tills. You go to Tesco, that's our homegrown system. When you use your scan-as-you-shop device, some of you might be shopping in Tesco, you use those handheld devices, completely synced, runs on the same platform.

Sources indicate that every single device runs on our platform. Cameras runs on our platform. Everything runs on our platform. Those are the core differentiator. Where we buy, platform integration is a must. That's how we say. Platform and domain boundaries. Now, centralization versus decentralization. The reason why I mentioned this here is if you're going through this space, and now even more so, 10 years on it's a different world with the agentic workforce that's coming. You can't centralize things. Gone are the days of change control board, architectural board, queue up in front of those pedestals and get your design reviewed and get your code reviewed and everything. We had to decentralize that. That's where we had to come up with very clear domain boundaries, good set of standards. Freedom within the guardrail, that's how we call it. Freedom within the framework with those guardrails to say how are we going to do it, and then you can decentralize that.

Industry observers note that tech excellence. Tech excellence is not just tech debt. We call it tech excellence, because it's proactive as well. It is not just, do we have a few bugs that we need to do? Or, do we need to patch our operating systems? Of course, yes. How are you taking care that you're not going to face into those challenges on an ongoing basis? Back then, there was no concept of total loss recovery. How do you plan for total loss recovery? This is not DR. DR is basic. When you're talking about total loss recovery, it's a completely different ballgame. The kinds of capabilities you need for that, we start to put that into tech excellence. Because it's very easily assumed, even within technology, and I'm not talking outside technology. Of course, business teams don't have that level of understanding. Even within technology, anyone who is not in engineering will assume that this gets done by some engineers who had a good coffee on a good day on the side of their desk.

It doesn't happen that way. You have to dedicate time for that. You have to dedicate focus for that. That requires education. Outside engineering, that requires education. Outside technology, as well, at some point. Where now our business leaders talk about tech excellence saying, are you sure it's built right? It's needed. That's the cultural change we are talking about. That creates the framework for a much faster pace of delivery and clear ownership, as I mentioned, with the clear domain boundaries, and strong and long-term resilience.

Sources indicate that that strategic framework gave us, what are the core tenets of our platform? Only customer is not enough. Yes, we are driven by customer. That drives our business. If you only think about customers, that's not enough. For the size of Tesco, when you've got almost half a million people working for you, colleague experience is equally needed. All the systems that we run in our stores, the operational systems that we run for our business operations, everything needed to be transformed, not just the customer-facing applications. Partners, we had very poor rating from our suppliers back then. We had to establish the trust, but also build the systems to make sure that our suppliers, partners, people who give us potatoes and tomatoes to sell for grocery, I'm referring to those partners, not tech partners, we had to improve experience for that. Reuse across multiple different markets and business units.

Sources indicate that offline operations. When you are talking about thousands of edge devices working in your stores, one of the most critical requirements for us is a network can be flaky. Because if you get in the business of replacing network of your entire thing, you might be spending hundreds of millions. Grocery is a very low margin business, it's around 4%. Some are 3%, some are 4%, some are 4.5%. It's a very low margin business. Every penny that you spend counts, goes in your P&L. Cyber risk and compliance built-in into the platform. Super important. This is where we had to innovate across all three public clouds. We did create private cloud, not just a server sitting in our data centers, and edge platform as well. As I was just referring to low margin business, cost is a feature for us, not a constraint. We don't see cost as a constraint.

According to recent reports, it's a very different mindset. As part of one of our learnings, we'll go through the learnings, but since we are talking about that, when we jumped into public cloud, and this now will apply into agentic code development as well, and we are thinking through that. The value that gets created against the cost that you might be spending, you've got to be very careful about that. We were spending upwards of £50 million, £60 million on public cloud. I'm talking four, five years back. It was growing exponentially. If you don't control that, then you've got £50 billion business, which was back then, with 4% margin, you're talking about £2 billion. When you talk £100 million of just cloud cost, I'm not talking our salaries, I'm not talking about entire technology department, this is just cloud cost. You can imagine how much P&L you are impacting at that level. It's the responsibility of the technology department to say, how do you keep cost as a feature, not as a constraint?

Sources indicate that then we came up with good principles for our platform, which, as I mentioned, domain design was very crucial. Create composable services. Data pathways and data quality both matter. You need very clear data pathways as to how data would flow between the various different operating datasets to data lakes, but also data quality across each one of these steps. Security in a layered defense model, all the way from perimeter to built inside. We got tons of different layers of how do you think about security. Multi-tenancy by default, which is, you build the platform once. Even from the physical deployment perspective is the same deployment that works and enables multiple countries for us, multiple different businesses. Build product capabilities, not just solutions, not point solutions. Build products, build capabilities. Then abstractions, all of you will understand that. It's not just for hiding complexity but also when you got mobile applications running across thousands of microservices, running in the data center or in the cloud.

For example, add an item to your shopping cart has got at least 40 different microservices called. Get the identity token, get the product ID, get the customer UUID, get their personalization preferences, get the price, check all that, get the product description. After that, it goes in the basket. Now if you are not creating abstractions that's going all the way from someone's mobile phone all the way to your data center or public cloud, and adding an item if it takes 40 network round trips, you are extremely slow. Yes, it is of course for hiding complexity, but at this scale all that matters. That's what went into our principles because that created cohesion across, as I was saying, digital and physical estate without becoming bottleneck.

Industry observers note that that was one of the lessons learned to say, while you are trying to do that, sometimes it's good to build more centralized capabilities first before you jump into that. It takes a little longer but saves you costly migration. From that perspective, any services that needs true elasticity and scalability we put it in public cloud. Public cloud is a dual-edged sword because when you start using PaaS, Platform as a Service, you get very tightly bound to that public cloud because many of them are very proprietary services. You will never get out of that. You lose your flexibility. As Tesco, at our scale, we like that flexibility. Whether it is when we buy the technologies for our use, deployed or in the cloud, anywhere, we care a lot about saying, does it give us flexibility or not? Because if you're not careful, the license fees keep on increasing exponentially.

If you are locked in, it's a very well-known fact that you will be held hostage. If you don't use PaaS then it's just a compute environment. Why are you in public cloud in the first place? You see, it works both ways. What we try to use is all portable PaaS technologies within the public cloud, that gives us that freedom. It's not perfect. I will not claim that. That does give us an optionality when it's needed. Then, many of our large systems, we are talking about supply chain systems, distribution centers, technologies related to that, we tend to run that into our private cloud. It's almost 80-20, 80% of our presence is in private cloud, 20% is in public cloud. Cost-wise, exact flip of that, 80% of the cost is in public cloud, 20% of the cost is in private cloud. It costs almost 8 to 10 times more for an equivalent setup in public cloud.

In a recent development, this is where as we are talking about agentic code development and everything, a developer could spend almost £500 a day without realizing or without clarity on what value is getting created. Again, if you step back historically this is where public cloud was almost 10 years back. Easy to jump in, hard to explain what value is getting created. The learnings here that we are talking while the technology will keep on evolving is pretty much where you can reapply.

Recent findings suggest that then comes the edge part of it. As I was saying, when you are at the scale and you want omni-channel experience, how do I now create a platform that is going to power your edge as well? What we did was, the same platform services, the microservices that run in our cloud, they run in our scaled environment with the right abstractions in our edge devices as well. There is a real consistency of business logic. There is a real consistency from data perspective, because when the network is there it's constantly exchanging data. For whatever reason, if the network is not available, we are able to identify the customer. If you have a club card, we identify your loyalty. We fail in favor of our customer. Let's say you did disable your club card literally last minute and network is chopped off and you are in the store, yes of course, that's a real-time requirement, but we fail in favor of our customers.

Industry observers note that we take the payment, not cash, credit card as well. Very lately we have enabled contactless payment as well. That's a huge set of capabilities. It's pretty much, you don't realize the store is running offline. The pricing on the shelf edge, that has to be considered. Now as many companies are talking about electronic shelf edge labels, that's part of our consideration in the platform, saying, what happens when the network is not running. How would you patch prices on the shelf edge labels? All this gets very taken for granted. Even I wasn't aware as to what's the level of complexity when you are in a retail business with hundreds of thousands of such devices running across thousands of stores. One part which we made sure was, it's the same team which is responsible for edge platform as well as our retail platform in the cloud. That made sure that consistency was there, that ownership was there.

In fact, when we were migrating from legacy stack and we were transforming, we made sure it's the same team that owned the legacy platform as well. You cannot compartmentalize and outsource the problem even within the technology department, saying, A team is building new services and A team will take care of the old services. Never works. You lose motivation very quickly.

According to recent reports, this is where we were talking about workload placement. We touched upon this a little bit before, which is, a single team owns that thing. We do use portable PaaS technologies when we are using the public cloud. In public cloud, we generally favor the systems that need scale and they are closer to the customer from that perspective. We, for the private environment in data centers, enabled the cloud as well so that for the developers it's the same experience when you are in the private cloud. We centralized a lot of our shared services. What initially started as, and this is probably a misconception, me being in technology, I'm 35 years in technology, that engineers love doing all these things. Setting up your Cassandra's, setting up your Kafka's, figuring out all the protocols. Yes, all that is true in the beginning part of the transformation. As we started putting more and more production workloads, because early on as part of our talent transformation we decided there is no separate QA team, there is no separate support team.

According to recent reports, of course, first-line support is different, but then pretty soon the call does come to our engineers so they are fully responsible for support of production environment. What started as a good challenge, as a good hobby, learning newly introduced technologies, pretty soon became very onerous. When I talk about creating shared services, so I own the retail platform, I own the tech platform, we'll talk about tech platform at Tesco, and I own the applications as well. It's not as much fun for engineers today to say, I'm going to deploy my own Cassandra, I will do the partitioning, and I will do all these things. It gets very onerous at some point. We invested a lot in shared services to say, how do you now not worry about all these things?

Sources indicate that the sequence is very important. When we started 10 years back, and we are talking about a company which is 100-plus years old, when we were talking about product development, the misconception in the business teams was, prepared meals in a box is called product. That was the journey when we started. When we started talking about platforms, we had to choose our sequence in the right way. You can never do Big Bang. You cannot ask a 50 billion business to stop and pause and say, we will come back in two years or one year or three years and we'll change everything. Even within that staggered approach, that you see from 2016, this is the real chart. In fact, we stopped counting at 2024, and we had only put significant items here. We had to pick our sequence. Initially it was very far and few in between. We had to develop and create that trust in technology from the business side to say, how are we going to figure this journey out.

Recent findings suggest that there was a lot of distrust when we started. You have to find the right demand, where the business demand, the customer demand is there, and find the right opportunities to do transformation in small steps early on, and then it gets bigger and bigger. Now we get more demand from the business with more trust, less questions. You say, how can we do it right?

We have been using AI for a very long time at Tesco. That's nothing upcoming for us. For example, start with all those business units I was saying, supply chain. One of the biggest challenges is forecasting how much customers would buy. If you go wrong in that one, it either leads to loss in millions or very poor customer experience. For example, if you forecast that you will sell 100kgs of tomatoes. It's in tons generally. I'm just taking an easy number. Except if you go wrong, either your shelves will be empty because customers are buying more and you need more than 100kg, or you will end up buying too much and it goes to waste. Waste is a substantial number. We try to control that, and we have done very well on that one. That's a tiny example, but that whole forecasting is dependent upon what's the lead time to getting the products.

In a recent development, like tomatoes can be supplied four times in a day in our distribution center. Something like jeans might be six months in advance. Then the shelf life could be very different. Tomatoes will get rotten in few days, non-perishable items will stay on the shelf for longer time, so the combination of that. That's the supply chain side. Distribution, how are you going to lay out all that stock? What's the stock management? What's the truck routing algorithms? Because we are talking about hundreds and thousands of miles of trucks traveling every day. How are you going to optimize that? Good for environment, good for firm, good for everyone. How do you fill the truck? This is just touching into the supply chain area. Likewise, when you talk about ranging, you talk about customer experience in personalization, you talk about pricing, everything is AI driven. How are we thinking about agentic commerce?

Because that changes the paradigm completely. What I remarked is agentic commerce is a business decision. Because if you don't participate in agentic commerce, you can be marginalized. Because, let's say most customers are spending time on ChatGPTs and Geminis of the world, and they are going into agentic commerce to say, we can do grocery for you. Of course, they want that. Nothing wrong in it. That's where customers are. If you don't go there, you can be marginalized. If you go there, you can still be marginalized because you're losing the first touch, customer experience. Because now you outsource that experience to someone else. Hence, it's a business decision. It's not just a technology decision. Getting ready requires complete shift. How would you be ready for agentic commerce? Because what used to be the simple SEO and SEM, the metadata and data on your website where the search engines will come and crawl your website and then you appear in the searches, organic search or paid search.

Recent findings suggest that now the agentic crawlers will come and you need much more machine-readable format of that data so that agents can understand. That's just the AEO, agentic understanding. We'll look at the architecture as to how you will prepare for that kind of integration. You will need the same kind of identity consent and policy frameworks as to how much you can allow the agents to operate on your website or through your APIs. Then multiple protocol interfaces are emerging, UCPs, ACPs. The platform completely evolves from a system of record, that's how it used to be, to a system of delegation. Because now those agents are working with your data, with your services, making decisions for the customer. It's a complete delegation.

That's the harness, how we are thinking. We are still going to use the platform because the core capabilities are still within our retail platform. If you look at the bottom left, customers, the bottom part is the existing path, existing online channels or stores from that perspective, existing application gateway, existing experience APIs going into our platform, retail platform. When you're talking about the agents on the top, you'll need now the gateways for the agents. How would you allow them? How much would you allow them? Which one would you allow them? The commerce protocol, ACP and UCP, now there are severe regulations in the UK for making payments, not allowed for agents to make payments on behalf of customers. Again, there are differences between the countries and regions to say what is allowed, what is not allowed. Many of these technologies, and I'm talking about both UCP, ACP, we are in direct conversation, are not ready for production scale yet.

As much as there is marketing, they are not ready. For Tesco scale, again you need very different readiness. We are not even talking about risk and compliance and anything here. I'm just talking pure technology risk here. Then you will have your own sub-agents that might be running, which might be talking to these agents and hence agent-to-agent protocol. You will need MCP for discovery of many of these services, discovery of data. Many of our application experience APIs were built for the applications that we built, like add item to basket, for example. You might need those plus some more for the agentic experience, but going back into the same retail platform. That's how we are looking into the future and thinking how we are going to do that.

Sources indicate that what could have been better is, build central tech platform early. As I mentioned, we jumped in early into the public cloud and then we realized that everyone had their own version of CI/CD platforms and observability and everything. Now when I was talking to my own teams, say, we got best CI/CD pipelines, and every team was saying that. I don't need 50 CI/CD pipelines, I need one CI/CD pipeline. Portfolio management, we introduced that a bit late, but that where the products are matured when you're talking about 6,000 people in technology and hundreds of products, you need a very good management of where you are going to put your investment, where the value is. The portfolio management becomes very important. We use product maturity model for that now to say, our product is mature or not mature, and it can go left and right in the maturity curve.

Location strategy. Most companies, they assume that engineering can be even in-sourced where they are your own teams. They can be in various different locations, but if you're not careful, product management sits somewhere else, engineering sits somewhere else, program sits somewhere else. Try to create self-sufficient teams. I touched on three parts of those transformation, a little bit of each one of them to say what's key. There are many more in that one. The biggest point was the more you step back and think about it, you will avoid costly re-implementation and migration. That's huge. It spends a lot of time and spend of cost.

Final two slides on what are some of the tips if you are following the transformation at scale. Three pillars, we talked about that. Just system transformation is not enough. Change business processes when required, because they are just organically developed like your technology systems as well. Question that to say, is that really different? Why should four different countries have different operational processes? Simplify operation. Build core capabilities, we just talked about that. Because now we have the tech platform which supports this retail platform for those same CI/CDs, the observabilities, everything, but we could have started that early. Start that early. Throughput is a long game. Today also we get a lot of pressures, and can we go live in two months? Can we go live in two weeks? Can we go live in three weeks? We can do that if the platform capabilities are there. Total throughput is much higher today, but the same thing could have taken us six months long back when we had to develop those capabilities.

If we didn't do that, now we can do 10 such things and we would never have done that because we would have just duplicated it. Evolve continuously. We used to be very horizontally laid. I ran entire engineering of Tesco, all the platforms, all this thing, but product management was separate. Now that platforms are matured, we are going more vertical. I still run the platforms because that we cannot divide. The core platform is still there, but the application domain wise now we are creating more partnership between business and people like me within technology. Evolution is necessary. E-commerce is not just enough. Avoid tech for tech. Communicate value early. It's very hard to understand outside technology for sure. What are you all doing, is the frequent question we get. How come you are so many people? What's going on? It has gone less and less now. Even within technology, it's hard to explain what value we have created for the business.

We talked about the cost, IP and vendor lock-in. We are very careful when we are talking about agentic code development. We are very careful as to what kind of IP leakage could happen. Vendor lock-in, we talked about it. Even when we use many of the SaaS solutions, we ask for those protections from data sharing perspective, from IP perspective, so that we keep that edge of differentiation for Tesco. Then last one is technology will keep evolving, but if you have set the right culture, I mean there was blockchain there, public cloud before that, MapReduce systems, now agentic part. It will keep happening, and the pace has increased. If you don't have the right culture, the right talent, and the right level of trust within the company, it won't work.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Huawei used its November 20, 2026 brand event to introduce OSTA (星芒), a fresh smartphone sub-brand, and launch the O1 Pro as a HarmonyOS AI phone with a starting list price of CNY 5,699.
  • Industry observers note that the newly introduced brand’s first handset makes Huawei’s own software and assistant its defining features.
  • Recent findings suggest that huawei’s Vmall listing labels the O1 Pro as a newly introduced product and lists the 12GB/256GB version at CNY 5,499, a CNY 200 discount from CNY 5,699.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Huawei used its November 20, 2026 brand event to introduce OSTA (星芒), a fresh smartphone sub-brand, and launch the O1 Pro as a HarmonyOS AI phone with a starting list price of CNY 5,699.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced brand’s first handset makes Huawei’s own software and assistant its defining features. The official product presentation introduces HarmonyOS 7 AI Pioneer Edition and Xiao Xingmang, an OSTA-specific interactive companion form of the Xiaoyi assistant.

Recent findings suggest that huawei’s Vmall listing labels the O1 Pro as a newly introduced product and lists the 12GB/256GB version at CNY 5,499, a CNY 200 discount from CNY 5,699. The range also offers 12GB/512GB, 16GB/512GB and 16GB/1TB configurations.

It has been revealed that huawei describes an interaction model in which the Xiaoyi AI screen is available immediately when the display is activated, using frequent usage scenarios and habits to present services proactively. Xiaoyi Space draws on likes, favorites and long-term memory, while natural-voice interaction supports continuous conversation and dialect recognition.

The product’s more consequential claim concerns execution. In Huawei’s coffee example, Xiaoyi uses location and preferences to recommend a drink, incorporates discounts and completes the order. #46625. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2057 w)
📖 Baca

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They write, summarize, translate, and call tools.
  • It has been revealed that say a customer calls your support line.
  • Recent findings suggest that in our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

It has been revealed that say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they stated (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

Recent findings suggest that in our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's upcoming speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It has been revealed that it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

Sources indicate that the steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Industry observers note that parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Sources indicate that downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

Recent findings suggest that when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

Industry observers note that the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

In a recent development, parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

According to recent reports, these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

It has been revealed that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't latest, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

It has been revealed that what's newly introduced is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

It has been revealed that urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

It has been revealed that if you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

It has been revealed that reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

It has been revealed that language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Recent findings suggest that each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Sources indicate that like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

According to recent reports, both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Complications and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

Tech Report: Stavros Gadinis, Berkeley Law Professor and Author of Corporate Ordering – Interview Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Johnson Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law.
  • Sources indicate that his new book, Corporate Ordering: How Corporations Navigate Social Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, examines how businesses develop governance systems when public rules are unsettled.
  • Industry observers note that your career spans corporate legal practice in Europe and research on corporate governance and financial regulation at Berkeley Law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stavros Gadinis is the George R. Johnson Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law. His research examines corporate governance, financial regulation, and the internal systems companies use to make and monitor decisions. Before entering academia, he practiced corporate law in Europe.

Sources indicate that his new book, Corporate Ordering: How Corporations Navigate Social Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, examines how businesses develop governance systems when public rules are unsettled. Through cases involving ridesharing, climate sustainability, and artificial intelligence, it considers how companies make rules, exercise authority, and oversee their own conduct.

Industry observers note that your career spans corporate legal practice in Europe and research on corporate governance and financial regulation at Berkeley Law. How did that background shape your thinking, and what inspired you to write Corporate Ordering?

According to recent reports, I began my career practicing corporate law in Europe, and then spent many years at Berkeley studying corporate governance and financial regulation, including how rules spread across borders when no single government is in charge. We tend to think of the business world and the regulatory world as opposites, one eager for quick decisions and large profits, the other committed to bureaucratic process and the public good. Practice and research both taught me that the line is much blurrier than that.

The book grew out of conversations with general counsel and senior executives about how they handle controversial decisions, the ones where employees, customers, communities and governments all want different things. What struck me is how closely their methods resemble those of a good regulator. They gather information by reaching out to the people affected, they explain their choices publicly, and they build mechanisms to check whether those choices hold up. These are not regulatory habits or corporate habits. They are the principles of sound decisionmaking in any institution that wields power over others. Corporate Ordering is my attempt to describe that machinery, show where it works, and show where it fails.

What is “corporate ordering,” and how does it help explain the way AI companies set rules for technologies that regulation has yet to catch up with?

It has been revealed that corporate ordering is the internal governance infrastructure companies build to make contested decisions before the law tells them what to do. It has three functions, which mirror the branches of a state. Rulemaking is how a tech giant writes its own principles. Executive action is how it applies them to concrete decisions. Monitoring is how it checks whether it followed through, and how it finds out when it did not.

Industry observers note that AI companies show all three at work. The frontier labs write constitutions, model specifications and safety frameworks, which is rulemaking. They decide whether a model is ready to launch, what it will refuse and who gets access, which is executive action. And they commission red-teaming, outside evaluations and incident reporting, which is monitoring. In the book I chart these functions across the major labs. The differences are real, but so is a striking convergence, as each firm discovers why it needs every piece.

Sources indicate that I want to be clear about one thing, because it is often misread. Corporate ordering is not an argument against regulation. It describes the material regulation will be built from. When legislators act, they borrow concepts the companies developed first. The real question is whether that first draft was written carefully enough to deserve borrowing.

Your book examines ridesharing, climate sustainability, and AI governance. Which lessons from the first two areas are most useful for AI, and where does AI present fundamentally different challenges?

In a recent development, the lesson from ridesharing and climate is that corporations very often write the first draft of the law. Uber and Lyft developed insurance and safety reporting practices before states had rules for them, and much of corporate carbon accounting runs on the GHG Protocol, a standard business helped build. Regulators then condoned those practices, supplemented them or wrote them into law. Regulation rarely starts from a blank slate. And the more thoughtful companies are about their choices, the more they take affected parties into account, the more likely those choices are to survive into regulation.

In a recent development, AI differs in two ways. The first is speed. Regulators are often a step behind industry, but in AI the gap is far wider. Regulators will have to look to companies to develop standards and internal processes, and concentrate their own efforts on oversight, verification and enforcement. That makes their role different, not smaller. Verification is where public power matters most, because it is where the conflict of interest with management is strongest. The second difference is reach. AI touches nearly every part of daily life, and it has become a major investment for the nation as a whole. The systemic risk implications are as hard to miss as they are to fathom.

When an AI tech giant selects and pays its own outside safety evaluators, what safeguards make that oversight meaningfully independent?

Industry observers note that this conflict of interest is familiar from financial auditing, and corporate law already has tools to manage it. The first is who hires and fires. The relationship with the evaluator should sit with independent directors who have no other financial ties to the tech giant, much as the audit committee, not the CEO or CFO, oversees the external auditor. Management should not be able to dismiss a reviewer whose findings are inconvenient.

Recent findings suggest that the second is access and publication. The evaluator needs to see what it asks to see, and it needs the right to publish its findings, or at least a meaningful summary, without a company veto. Reputational risk is what gives a review its teeth. The third is common review standards, so that an evaluation means the same thing across firms and evaluators cannot compete by being lenient. The fourth is protection for whistleblowers, and even rewards when they bring actionable information, because people inside the company are often the first to know when an evaluation was steered.

Suppose an outside evaluator identifies a serious safety concern just before a major model launch. Who should receive that finding, and who should have the authority to delay or stop deployment?

The finding should go to the board directly, ideally to a committee of independent directors responsible for safety, and not only through the management team that is pushing for the launch. Management can and should respond, but it should not be the filter. The authority to delay or stop deployment should rest with the board, because this is exactly the kind of decision boards exist to make, one with large stakes, conflicting interests and no obvious right answer.

But the more notable point is that the decision must be explicit and documented, and traceable to the people who made it. If the board goes ahead despite the concern, the record should show what it knew, what it weighed and why it judged the risk acceptable. That paper trail creates the conditions for liability, or at least reputational damage, and it makes people think twice. Courts are increasingly willing to recognize that design choices in software have consequences for users, and a organization that can show a serious, documented effort stands in a very different position from one that cannot.

When safety concerns conflict with revenue targets or competitive pressure, what should a credible board decision-making process look like?

According to recent reports, A credible process is an informed one, and it leaves a record. The board should see concrete information about the costs of delay, the nature and likelihood of the safety concern, and the options for mitigating it. It should ask whether the testing was adequate and, where it was not, commission more or invite outside review. Where real uncertainty remains, there are options between launching and shelving, such as a limited release, a staged rollout or a sandbox, that let the firm learn more before it commits. And whatever the board decides, what the company then indicates publicly about the model’s safety must be accurate, which is where much of the current litigation risk lies.

It has been revealed that then the board should write down what it decided and why. Over time those records become a body of precedent, so the next hard call is measured against the last one, and anyone reviewing the company can see whether its stated principles actually bind. Microsoft has started to build this kind of decision record, and I think it is one of the most underrated tools in AI governance. Competitive pressure is real, and a board may reasonably decide to move ahead. What it cannot do is decide by default.

Your work proposes a “social business judgment” standard for evaluating board decisions. How would that apply to an AI company that postpones a profitable product launch because of potential public harm?

Under existing corporate law, a board that postpones a profitable launch is already well protected. Courts defer to directors’ business judgment, and accepting lower profits today to avoid harm tomorrow fits comfortably within it. The harder question runs the other way, whether the board took public harm seriously at all.

Social business judgment asks the board to evaluate potential public harm the way it evaluates any other business risk, through tangible, measurable and specific metrics wherever possible. The emphasis is on process and due diligence, not on the outcome. A board that sources the right information, hears from those affected and records its reasoning has earned deference, whether it postpones the launch or proceeds with it. A board that does none of this has not. So in the case you describe, the postponement itself is not the concern. The issue is whether the board can show how it reached that decision, and whether it would reach the same one again on the same facts.

AI companies publish safety frameworks and voluntary commitments, but readers rarely see how those policies affect individual decisions. What evidence would distinguish effective governance from a public relations exercise?

Very often, when companies publish frameworks, the public is left wondering whether the framework ever applies to specific decisions or remains rhetoric the firm never follows through on. The answer is disclosure of a particular kind. Rather than more statements of principle, companies should report the specific choices they made and how the framework shaped them, which rolls out were delayed, which capabilities were held back, which risk thresholds were triggered and what followed.

Sources indicate that the most telling evidence is a decision that cost the company something. A framework that has never changed an outcome, never delayed a launch and never been invoked against revenue is hard to distinguish from public relations. These disclosures also need to be specific enough to verify, and for the most consequential questions they should be verified by a third party with the standing to say so publicly.

Sources indicate that where does corporate self-governance reach its limits? Which decisions about acceptable AI risk require public rules or democratic oversight?

The most crucial limit has to do with failures to monitor. Even a well-intentioned, responsible manufacturer can face a major crisis, and at that moment conflicts of interest multiply. Employees may withhold information that would hurt their jobs or their bonuses. Executives may suppress bad news to avoid public criticism. Fear of lawsuits may keep the company from being open. In past corporate crises, the crucial information usually came from people leadership could not control, external auditors and reviewers, affected parties, or internal whistleblowers using independent reporting channels.

This is where public rules matter most. The law can add relatively little at the rulemaking stage, because statutes tend to borrow their key concepts from the companies. It can add more on disclosure, by reaching firms that will not disclose voluntarily. And it adds the most on verification, by requiring independent review, protecting whistleblowers and giving outside checks real authority.

The other limit is collective. The most a single company can do is stop itself. It cannot stop its competitors. Decisions about catastrophic risk, including whether to slow the frontier, require coordination across firms and governments, at home and internationally. One model I find promising is an international standard-setter along the lines of the ISSB in sustainability reporting, independent of governments but overseen by trustees that include them. Corporate ordering is necessary for this work, because the taming of these models happens inside the companies that build them, but it cannot carry the work alone.

If you were advising the board of a fast-growing AI company today, what three governance changes would you prioritize, and what evidence would you look for a year later to determine whether they worked?

First, outreach in rulemaking. Before adopting or revising its safety framework or usage policies, the company should consult the people affected (users, civil society, domain experts) and publish what it heard and how it responded. Second, regular responsibility reporting, an annual account of the hard decisions the board and management made under the framework, with enough detail to be checked. Third, an external monitor, hired by and reporting to independent directors, with full access and the right to publish.

According to recent reports, A year later I would look for evidence that each one actually bit. For outreach, at least one rule that changed because of what the company heard. For reporting, disclosed decisions the company would rather not have discussed, including ones that cost it revenue or time. For the monitor, findings the company did not want, and a record of what the board did about them. If after a year everything reported is good news, the changes have not worked.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore the book and purchase options should visit the official website for Corporate Ordering.

OpenAI Introduces MedChemBench for Medicinal-Chemistry Reasoning

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI introduced MedChemBench, a 99-problem medicinal-chemistry benchmark, on November 20, 2026, and reported that GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of available credit at the xhigh reasoning-effort setting.
  • According to recent reports, the other reported xhigh scores were 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol.
  • In a recent development, the technical paper describes a retrospective set of tasks drawn from 117 papers and patents, encompassing 761 distinct graded molecular structures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI introduced MedChemBench, a 99-problem medicinal-chemistry benchmark, on November 20, 2026, and reported that GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of available credit at the xhigh reasoning-effort setting. It tests whether models can connect molecular structures with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds and predict properties.

According to recent reports, the other reported xhigh scores were 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol. The benchmark addresses a central difficulty in medicinal chemistry: a compound can be potent against a disease-related protein while being poorly absorbed or metabolized too quickly. Selecting what to test next therefore requires weighing competing properties rather than optimizing one measurement.

In a recent development, the technical paper describes a retrospective set of tasks drawn from 117 papers and patents, encompassing 761 distinct graded molecular structures. Prompts generally stop at a selected decision point in a research program, providing the biological context, earlier compounds and selected experimental findings. Later results are withheld to inform reference answers and grading criteria.

The tasks cover preclinical drug discovery, not clinical development, across seven categories. These include integrated lead selection with 48 tasks, structure–activity relationship forecasting with 26, and smaller groups covering ADME (absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion) and delivery, molecular design and enumeration, safety and liabilities, retrosynthesis, and assay biology and mechanism. Eighty-five tasks span more than one scientific-content domain, reflecting how a lead choice can depend simultaneously on potency, selectivity, cell assays, metabolism, exposure and safety.

One problem concerning PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery, asks models to reconstruct three related compounds and predict cellular potency, permeability, efflux and human microsomal clearance. The withheld results illustrate the tradeoff: compound 23 was more potent in cells, while compound 24 crossed a cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in a liver-enzyme assay.

Sources indicate that grading combines deterministic checks with model-judged rubrics. Molecular structure and scientific rationale account for 37.49% and 35.78% of available credit, respectively; ranking and candidate selection account for 17.51%, and numerical or categorical prediction for 8.92%. For structures, RDKit converts submitted SMILES, a text representation of molecular graphs, into canonical isomeric form while preserving stereochemistry and isotopes. Numerical predictions generally receive partial credit based on fold error, while a separate GPT-6 Astra judge at medium reasoning effort scores scientific-rationale criteria as zero, half or full credit.

Across 11 GPT models and 61 model–effort conditions, the paper reports 60,390 graded responses, with ten retained responses for each task in every condition. GPT-6.2 Astra is not among those 11 models; its result comes from the announcement.

Sources indicate that at xhigh, the paper reports that GPT-6 Astra earned 95.37% of available molecular-structure credit and 91.05% of scientific-rationale credit, compared with 50.42% for ranking and candidate selection and 47.02% for numerical prediction. The components cover different applicable tasks and scoring rules, but the results distinguish strong reconstruction and explanation from weaker compound selection and quantitative forecasting.

A reconstruction task described in the paper makes the structural differences concrete. Models had to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. GPT-6 Astra produced the correct compound in all ten xhigh responses, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna failed in all ten of theirs. The illustrated Sol answer contained a 15-atom ring, while Luna returned two disconnected fragments. Such errors change the molecule’s identity before any property reasoning begins.

According to recent reports, openAI states that the scores do not establish whether models can discover newly introduced drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Every answer was a single attempt without tools, feedback or new experiments, and the tasks use historical evidence rather than prospective discovery. Prior exposure to the published sources also cannot be ruled out.

For a heuristic check, the authors added source DOI or patent identifiers to all 99 prompts for nine models at xhigh. Mean overall-score changes ranged from a 0.23-percentage-point decrease to a 0.80-point increase, and every model-specific 95% confidence interval included zero. The check cannot establish whether source material appeared in training data.

Sources indicate that the paper describes MedChemBench as close to saturation in its current form and states open-ended design and synthesis grading remains partly tied to reference answers, which may penalize plausible alternatives. Proposed extensions include prospective cases, expert adjudication of alternative answers, explicit treatment of assay uncertainty, and an agent-based track allowing retrieval, calculation, structure verification and multistep revision.

MedChemBench therefore separates chemical comprehension from demonstrated drug-discovery impact. Its strongest results concern reconstructing and explaining fixed historical problems, while compound selection and numerical forecasting lag. The proposed prospective and agent-based evaluations address the resulting open question: whether models can make better research decisions when they must gather evidence, calculate properties and revise their answers over multiple steps.

According to recent reports, with a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.
