Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

In a recent development, mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

It has been revealed that for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • METR reported on November 20, 2026, that public frontier models’ 50% time horizons—the human-estimated task duration at which a model is predicted to succeed half the time, not how long the model itself works—are doubling roughly every 110 days across its combined TH1.1 and TH2 evaluations.
  • The upgrade covers public models through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra and examines capabilities relevant to automating AI research and development (R&D).
  • Industry observers note that METR estimates a 95% confidence interval of 2.08 to 4.94 months for the combined doubling time, close to the previous 105-day trend for TH1.1 alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

METR reported on November 20, 2026, that public frontier models’ 50% time horizons—the human-estimated task duration at which a model is predicted to succeed half the time, not how long the model itself works—are doubling roughly every 110 days across its combined TH1.1 and TH2 evaluations. The expanded testing indicates strong gains on verifiable work but weaker judgment on open-ended research and evaluation design.

The upgrade covers public models through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra and examines capabilities relevant to automating AI research and development (R&D). METR typically evaluated 15 models on TH1.1 and TH2. The new TH2 suite contains 36 tasks in 12 families: eight verifiable families with well-defined, automatically scored objectives across optimization, machine learning, puzzles and games, and four families covering conceptual reasoning, judgment and open-ended research without a cheap check for success.

Industry observers note that METR estimates a 95% confidence interval of 2.08 to 4.94 months for the combined doubling time, close to the previous 105-day trend for TH1.1 alone. Because TH2 is harder at a fixed human task duration, a model’s 50% time horizon on the combined suite is lower than on TH1.1 alone.

On TH2’s verifiable subset, the estimated doubling time falls to 1.65 months, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.79 to 3.99 months. METR cautions that this noisy result could reflect task composition, a restricted date range or selection during task development rather than broad acceleration. Less diverse task sets may also produce faster doubling because longer tasks require more of the same skills.

Human calibration is less direct than in METR’s earlier work. Researchers defined score-and-time thresholds for 34 of the latest tasks, using successful human baselines for three and researcher estimates for 31; direct baselines informed only 9% of human-duration estimates. The specialists were paid $200 to $350 per hour and could use Sonnet 5 for implementation. METR reports similar doubling-time results after adding noise to task-time estimates and substituting model-estimated human completion times, though it remains uncertain how comparable the baseliners were to frontier-lab researchers.

Sources indicate that on verifiable TH2 tasks, METR estimates current public frontier models’ time horizons at up to 27 hours. On each of the three formally baselined tasks, the best model outperformed every recruited human baseliner.

It has been revealed that larger pools of human data show that top experts can still finish ahead. Across 15 Al Zimmermann optimization contests, METR reports that the strongest models placed at the 96th to 98th percentile of human participants in the median contest, while roughly four humans beat them. Agents had 48 hours on a 28-core machine; human participants had about three months and their own hardware, so the rankings depend on those different conditions.

On Budget NanoGPT, METR reports a best autonomous-agent speedup of 15.7% in 48 hours, compared with a 41% speedup over the previous record by a recent AI-assisted human contributor who estimated spending about 60 hours. The comparison is rough because human records build sequentially on earlier work, but it shows autonomous agents trailing the strongest human result while exceeding many other competent speedrunners.

The hard-to-verify tasks reveal a different limitation. In Making METR Tasks, agents had to design an informative new task for METR’s own suite. METR classified some recent outputs as borderline useful, but none warranted inclusion in the suite used in the report. Models generally created automatically scored optimization tasks even when instructed to emphasize decisions with poor short-term feedback. Despite internet access, they did not independently investigate what METR would find useful, produce novel threat modeling, or base tasks on particularly insightful hypotheses about model capabilities. Those ratings rest on METR’s own research and threat-modeling judgments.

According to recent reports, A related experiment examined whether models could score those outputs reliably. METR found that model judges agreed more closely with human ratings when assessing weaker models’ outputs, but awarded inappropriately high scores to work from similarly strong or stronger models. Opus 5.5, the judge with the highest human agreement, scored GPT-6 Astra’s tasks about 0.2 points higher than the human scorer on a one-point scale.

In a recent development, these results do not establish a universal judgment deficit. METR notes models may be underelicited on judgment tasks because they underused token limits and available affordances, and notes that frontier models displayed good judgment of unclear generality on some programmatically scored machine-learning tasks.

According to recent reports, the measurement problem extends beyond judgment. METR is concerned that containerized evaluations may resemble the reinforcement-learning environments used to train models, potentially overstating real-world capabilities as similar environments become common in training.

Sources indicate that lifecycle Cost is a rough, model-estimated proxy for developing a containerized task environment and running and scoring it 100 times, rather than a direct estimate of an AI developer’s training-environment costs. After controlling for task length, METR found the higher-cost subset was 2.9 times as expensive as the lower-cost subset on average, while models performed 2.9 times worse by time horizon, equivalent to 1.5 doublings. Models nevertheless improved at similar rates on the two subsets, so the data associates cost with difficulty without showing slower progress on costlier tasks.

METR reports no strong overall acceleration or deceleration across the tested public frontier on its separate METR Capability Index, which summarizes model performance on a common scale. Developer-specific slope changes were sensitive to methodological choices, leaving their validity uncertain.

Recent findings suggest that METR nevertheless says current public evidence is insufficient to rule out drastic AI R&D acceleration in the next couple of years, defined as capabilities improving so swiftly that humans can no longer meaningfully understand, assess and react to catastrophic risks from upcoming systems. Which capabilities would produce that outcome remains unknown, and easy-to-verify tasks alone might suffice. The findings therefore make weaker judgment a plausible constraint on research automation, not proof that acceleration must wait for models to perform well on realistic tasks associated with ordinary jobs.

With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Latest Update: Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale.
  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.
  • According to recent reports, google has announced it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two important components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

According to recent reports, google has announced it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two important components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance. The move is intended to address two emerging challenges in running autonomous agents at scale: securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing the substantial compute overhead created by agents that frequently pause and resume.

Industry observers note that the announcement also includes OpenRL, Google's open-source reinforcement learning orchestration project. Together, the projects target different layers of agent infrastructure, from isolated code execution to managing agent lifecycles and coordinating large-scale training workloads. The goal is to establish an open foundation for agentic applications, much as Kubernetes helped standardise container orchestration.

Google argues that conventional Kubernetes workloads and AI agents have fundamentally different execution patterns.

In a recent development, A traditional application typically starts, serves requests, and continues running. An AI agent, however, may execute a tool or code for a few seconds before waiting for model inference, an external API, or human approval. Google estimates that agents can spend 90-95% of their time idle while still holding vital state, including memory, files, repositories, and active sessions.

Keeping every agent in a dedicated Pod wastes resources, while scaling to zero introduces delays when environments must be reconstructed. At the other extreme, large-scale agent evaluations can overwhelm Kubernetes control planes when thousands of short-lived execution environments are repeatedly created and destroyed.

Google developed Agent Substrate to address these limitations by separating agent state (actors) from the compute resources (workers) used to execute it.

Actors represent individual agent sessions and retain their state, including filesystem contents, memory, and execution context. Workers provide reusable, pre-warmed execution environments drawn from shared Kubernetes pools.

Industry observers note that when an agent needs to resume, Substrate assigns it to an available Worker and restores its previous state. When the agent becomes idle, its state can be saved and the underlying compute resource released.

Industry observers note that according to Google, this approach lets agents resume in under 500 milliseconds without creating a new Kubernetes Pod for every execution. It also reduces pressure on the Kubernetes control plane by managing agent lifecycles independently of individual Pod objects.

The second major challenge is security. AI agents routinely execute generated shell commands, install packages, and interact with external tools. Treating this code as trusted creates significant risks, particularly when multiple agents share infrastructure.

Google's gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary through a user-space application kernel. Instead of letting containerised applications interact directly with the host Linux kernel, gVisor intercepts system calls and handles them within its own isolated environment.

This reduces the exposure of the underlying host while retaining much of the efficiency associated with container-based execution.

Agent Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs for workloads requiring hardware-level virtualisation. This gives platform teams flexibility to select an appropriate isolation boundary without changing the overall agent lifecycle model.

According to recent reports, the announcement reflects a broader shift in cloud-native infrastructure. Kubernetes was designed around long-running applications and relatively stable workloads. Agentic systems introduce more dynamic execution patterns, where environments must be created, suspended, restored, and isolated at much greater frequency.

Recent findings suggest that other providers are addressing similar challenges through technologies such as Kata Containers, Firecracker, and dedicated sandboxing platforms. Google's contribution is to combine secure execution with an agent-aware orchestration model and place the resulting technologies within an open ecosystem.

In a recent development, the wider implication is that AI agents need more than an orchestration framework and access to tools; they need their own secure, stateful, and efficiently managed execution infrastructure. By donating these projects to the CNCF, Google is helping establish the foundations for that next layer of cloud-native computing.

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Industry observers note that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Industry observers note that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

According to recent reports, the U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

According to recent reports, but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

According to recent reports, the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many upcoming science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. Newly introduced public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an key part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved notable in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support fresh research that others can build upon.

According to recent reports, this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

According to recent reports, making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an notable first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

According to recent reports, to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Sources indicate that participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

According to recent reports, the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be revealed through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or firm building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

OpenAI Strengthens GPT-6.2 Astra Against Reasoning Extraction

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI on November 20, 2026 announced stronger defenses against adversarial distillation, reporting that the average success rate for adaptive attacks extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request fell from 54.0% on GPT-6 Astra with original safeguards to 0.2% on GPT-6.2 Astra with updated safeguards.
  • For extraction from the current request, the corresponding average fell from 22.9% to 0.9%, OpenAI reports.
  • Protected reasoning is the intermediate chain-of-thought a model generates while working toward an answer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI on November 20, 2026 announced stronger defenses against adversarial distillation, reporting that the average success rate for adaptive attacks extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request fell from 54.0% on GPT-6 Astra with original safeguards to 0.2% on GPT-6.2 Astra with updated safeguards.

For extraction from the current request, the corresponding average fell from 22.9% to 0.9%, OpenAI reports. The adaptive black-box evaluation aggregates results across six attacker models, with automated red-teamers adjusting their approach as the system responds and seeing only what an external user would see. The strengthened protections cover GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, and selected improvements are also being applied to GPT-6 Astra.

Protected reasoning is the intermediate chain-of-thought a model generates while working toward an answer. These traces can contain information omitted from final responses, making them especially valuable to adversarial distillation, which uses a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another system. The resulting model may reproduce dual-use capabilities without the safeguards that constrained the original.

OpenAI’s internal study compared two training runs from the same pretrained student model, the learner in a setup where a teacher model produces the training data. One run used exact teacher reasoning traces; the other used the user-visible baseline of final responses, reasoning summaries and tool interactions. The fine-tuning data consisted primarily of Astra-level teacher trajectories on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Students were evaluated after supervised fine-tuning and again after lightweight reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.

It has been revealed that after supervised fine-tuning, the exact-trace student generally outperformed the summary-trained student, OpenAI reports. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student scored higher at the largest tested inference budget on both reported benchmarks, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.

OpenAI interprets the results as evidence that protecting exact traces can limit cyber-capability transfer even when the underlying tasks are permitted under its usage policies, while saying it will continue studying transfer across different student models and training recipes. Across many such interactions, exact traces can teach skills that generalize beyond the teacher’s original tasks.

Industry observers note that at the request level, adversarial training teaches models to recognize extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning while preserving legitimate explanations and assistance. Input classifiers look for extraction attempts, while output classifiers inspect assistant messages and tool-call arguments in streaming and non-streaming responses. Tool-call coverage matters because reasoning can appear in a tool’s arguments without appearing in the final answer; output classifiers can block suspected leaks before they reach the caller.

According to recent reports, the updated API ties protected reasoning in GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to the conversation history that produced it. A model can build on earlier reasoning as messages are added, but rewriting an earlier message drops the reasoning that followed it. Older model families with weaker safeguards cannot read the two models’ protected reasoning, restricting reuse across model-family boundaries.

Industry observers note that campaign-level defenses use request and account signals to investigate coordinated extraction, and attacks uncovered during investigations become examples for safeguard training and testing. OpenAI noted weekly enforcement actions against unauthorized distillation campaigns in 2026 have ranged from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly during summer 2026. The organization tracks abuse prevalence and detection-to-enforcement time, aiming to reduce the data attackers obtain, raise campaign costs and shorten response times.

The announcement follows OpenAI’s September 30, 2026 disclosure of a coordinated campaign first observed on July 1, 2026. The earlier report described 16,000 attempted extraction requests from more than 4,000 owners on July 24 and 25, 2026, attributed a core cluster to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, and stated it was unclear whether all operators belonged to one actor.

OpenAI shares indicators of compromise with other model providers and works with deployment partners on safeguard requirements and coordinated enforcement. Its recommendations for other developers include checking assistant messages and tool-call arguments, restricting encrypted-reasoning reuse across conversations and models, retaining successful attacks as regression tests for future safeguards, and pairing request controls with campaign investigations. The organization plans to share more about recently disrupted campaigns.

OpenAI has told Congress it supports the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act and the MATCH Act, alongside broader legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors illicitly extracting capabilities from American AI models.

The manufacturer argues that export controls and distillation defenses address different parts of that risk: export controls limit access to hardware needed to train frontier models, while distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained.

For model providers, the practical security boundary extends beyond final answers to how reasoning is reused across conversations, exposed through tool calls and monitored across accounts. The study also suggests that permitted coding and defensive-cybersecurity tasks can create a capability-transfer risk, making interaction-wide protection and campaign enforcement parts of the same defense.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, 2026, an open-weights model built to run on consumer laptops.
  • Industry observers note that the full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and a companion research model, TML-d24-varloop-research, are available on Hugging Face.
  • According to recent reports, A organization demonstration shows Inkling 2 Mini running offline on a MacBook Pro in airplane mode during a flight, where it built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, 2026, an open-weights model built to run on consumer laptops. It has 26.4 billion total parameters and a memory footprint of about 20GB, using repeated passes through its middle layers to improve reasoning.

Industry observers note that the full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and a companion research model, TML-d24-varloop-research, are available on Hugging Face. Tinker offers inference and fine-tuning, with chat in Tinker Playground, while local options include Ollama on Mac systems with at least 32GB of RAM and GGUF versions through Unsloth and llama.cpp.

According to recent reports, A organization demonstration shows Inkling 2 Mini running offline on a MacBook Pro in airplane mode during a flight, where it built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes. Another demonstration uses one offline MacBook to power all 20 residents of Thinkyville, a simulated pixel town, illustrating how multiple persistent agents can run locally.

Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts transformer, meaning only a subset of its specialized components is used for each token. Its 24 layers are divided into four blocks of six. The first and last blocks run once, while the two middle blocks share weights and run three times, producing 48 layer applications per token from 24 stored layers. The model has 3.4 billion active parameters and 5.4 billion weight activations per token once looping is included.

Recent findings suggest that attention residuals let each layer learn its own mixture of earlier block outputs instead of adding every output into a single running sum. The second and third passes also receive a gated message from the preceding pass. That gate initially blocks the message and learns to admit more of it during training, allowing looping to be introduced without destabilizing the model.

In the firm’s training comparison, an unpruned non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train but required 140% more inference compute to match the looped version’s loss on 512,000-token agentic traces.

Training began with 384 experts and eight selected per token. Two-thirds were pruned during midtraining, leaving the 128 most-used experts in each layer, after which the model trained on 1 trillion tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model to recover its earlier performance. Twenty layers were trained and are deployed in 4-bit NVFP4, with the final four in 8-bit MXFP8; the company says matching training and deployment precision avoids conversion loss from post-training quantization.

According to recent reports, thinking Machines Lab reports scores of 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 77.9% on the 51-task SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard evaluation, compared with 42.2% and 73.8% for Qwen3.8-27B, respectively, alongside 46.5% on Vals Index v2.2. Its comparison notes that evaluation setups vary by model.

The company says looping improves reasoning without enabling the weights to store more facts; knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s AA-Omniscience result is in line with other models of its size, while its leads among similar-sized open-weights models on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA and MCP Atlas come from efficient use of search and tools.

In a recent development, the firm also claims Inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or instructions with many constraints, reporting 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1. It trails larger models on reasoning-intensive benchmarks including CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.

It has been revealed that looping complicates chain-of-thought monitoring, the practice of reading a model’s written reasoning to oversee its behavior. A conventional transformer must externalize reasoning that needs additional sequential steps; a looped model can perform more of those steps internally before producing text. Reasoning that never enters the text cannot be inspected by that kind of monitor.

It has been revealed that because Inkling 2 Mini supports only a fixed number of passes, the lab trained TML-d24-varloop-research with one to five passes, mostly three, and conducted reinforcement learning at three. On a Think Fast subset, the tech giant reports that its no-chain-of-thought time horizon, defined as the human completion time of tasks it can finish at 50% reliability without written reasoning, rose from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds at three before roughly flattening. N-Hop Lookup accuracy continued improving through ten loops even though training had not exceeded five passes.

In a recent development, in the company’s initial analysis of GPQA Diamond questions answered correctly at every tested depth, average reasoning traces fell from 3,703 tokens at one pass to 1,661 at five. Mean sentence length changed only from 8.9 to 8.7 words, and the share of words found in an English dictionary moved from 94.6% to 94.4%; the shorter traces were more direct and involved less backtracking.

The agentic tests used a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-loop model in LinuxArena. With Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as a weaker monitor, the firm found no clear trend in stealth rate as loop count increased; restricting the monitor to tool calls and outputs left a significant number of attacks undetected.

It has been revealed that these monitorability results are preliminary. Reinforcement learning only at three passes means the experiments do not establish what a model trained at higher pass counts would learn, and the company cautions that such a model might compress its reasoning more aggressively.

According to recent reports, for oversight researchers, the open question is whether the legibility observed at this scale survives larger models and training regimes that optimize deeper loops. The fixed and variable open-weights releases provide a direct way to investigate that question across looping depths.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

Sources indicate that uber has redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while keeping p99 cache miss latency below one millisecond. The hybrid architecture retains translation keys and frequently accessed values in memory while storing the remaining values on disk. The system serves millions of translations per second and maintains a cache hit rate above 99.9%.

The optimization addresses two problems identified through memory profiling across Uber's Go services. Garbage collection (GC) consumed more than 20% of CPU utilization in some services, with translations accounting for approximately 70% of allocated objects.

At Uber's scale, even small inefficiencies in memory management can add up.

According to recent reports, the first optimization replaced Go's sync.Map with a conventional map[string]string protected by an RWMutex. The workload was predominantly read-heavy, with infrequent updates and no individual deletions. The previous implementation created multiple objects and pointers for each translation entry, increasing GC overhead. Moving to a value-based map reduced object allocations and improved CPU utilization by more than 30% in the affected service.

However, reducing object allocations did not solve the overall memory consumption problem. Translation datasets could contain two to three million keys, although individual services typically accessed only a small subset. Cache refreshes introduced another glitch: the service built a replacement cache in the background before atomically swapping it with the existing one. Both copies therefore occupied memory simultaneously, causing some services to run out of memory during refreshes.

Sources indicate that uber considered external caching and generating service-specific translation subsets, but both introduced additional operational or maintenance costs. The team instead adopted a hybrid storage design that preserves the existing Get() and Put() API. All keys remain available in memory for fast lookups, while translation values are stored in disk-backed files.

Uber's hybrid translation cache (Source: Uber Blog Post).

According to recent reports, the implementation uses 256 shards, each with its own read-write mutex, in-memory entries, and disk file. Six-byte hash-based keys reduce metadata overhead, with a fallback to the original key format to handle collisions. A time-based global least recently used (LRU) policy manages in-memory entries. During cache refreshes, the system uses access history to preload translations accessed within the previous 15 minutes, avoiding a cold cache after the swap.

Sources indicate that in one example, a translation dataset that previously consumed approximately 800 MB in memory required around 40 MB for metadata after the redesign. With a configured limit of 50,000 in-memory entries, actual memory consumption typically ranged between 80 MB and 120 MB. In another reported workload, approximately 30,000 of more than four million entries were loaded in memory, while the cache hit rate remained above 99.9%. The p99 latency for disk-backed cache misses stayed below 100 microseconds.

Memory usage decreased from approximately 2.7 GB to 750 MB (Source: Uber Blog Post).

Industry observers note that uber's experience highlights the cost implications of in-memory caching at scale. The team recommends minimizing object references to reduce GC overhead and measuring how frequently cached values are accessed. When only a small proportion of cached data is actively used, a hybrid approach can retain frequently accessed values in memory while moving the rest to disk.

Industry News: Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • According to recent reports, transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

According to recent reports, transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

Recent findings suggest that the integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Sources indicate that our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

In a recent development, A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

According to recent reports, A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

It has been revealed that we replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

Sources indicate that we then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

Sources indicate that we also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report demonstrates what this looks like on a significant model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a newly introduced model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

According to recent reports, it drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a upcoming model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

It has been revealed that we used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Industry observers note that with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

Sources indicate that so we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

It has been revealed that the Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

Industry observers note that as of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the research by graduate student Sunbochen Tang and professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis concerns models of weather, climate, turbulence and other nonlinear processes.
  • Chaotic systems are highly sensitive to initial conditions, so tiny differences can produce dramatically different outcomes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that MIT researchers have developed a machine-learning framework that guarantees bounded trajectories for AI models of chaotic systems, addressing simulations that can drift into physically impossible values during long runs. MIT revealed the work on November 20, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the research by graduate student Sunbochen Tang and professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis concerns models of weather, climate, turbulence and other nonlinear processes. Their paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences was published online on October 12, 2026, and appeared in the journal’s October 20, 2026, matter.

Chaotic systems are highly sensitive to initial conditions, so tiny differences can produce dramatically different outcomes. A neural network may match data over a short period and still fail when left to run: small errors can accumulate until its simulated values grow without limit, even though the real system remains bounded. That behavior can invalidate estimates of long-term statistics, a central goal of modeling dissipative chaotic systems.

The guarantee therefore concerns long-term bounded behavior rather than exact point-by-point forecasting far into the future. It seeks to preserve valid long-run statistics without suppressing the complicated variation that makes the system chaotic. As Azizan put it, “Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.”.

Recent findings suggest that the framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator, which predicts how the system evolves, and an energy-like representation. That representation is used to construct an algebraic dissipative constraint inside a projection layer, which adjusts the model’s predicted evolution. Outside a learned boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, drawing trajectories toward the bounded region while allowing chaotic behavior within it.

The paper says this construction enforces dissipation by design and provides formal trajectory-boundedness guarantees over arbitrarily long forecast windows. The learned energy boundary also supplies an outer estimate of the system’s strange attractor, whose complex geometry makes it difficult to characterize directly.

Tang mentioned soft penalties or incentives applied during training need not hold when a deployed model faces new inputs, so unbounded predictions remain possible. Arbitrary caps can keep outputs within a chosen limit, but they can also restrict the model’s ability to represent complex features that should be learned from data. The projection layer is modular and model-agnostic, allowing it to work with different neural-network architectures.

MIT reports that the approach closely tracked true outcomes in tests ranging from textbook systems to complex multidimensional cases, while conventional methods moved into impossible predictions. The published demonstrations include Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation, where the method produced bounded long-horizon forecasts that preserved invariant statistics.

According to recent reports, A related Energy-Constrained Operator paper by Andrea Goertzen, Tang and Azizan was published on June 7, 2026. It introduced a closed-form quadratic projection layer and reported stable long-horizon forecasts that captured invariant statistics for systems governed by the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky and Navier–Stokes equations. Both papers use control-theoretic energy conditions to tackle predictions whose unbounded growth prevents meaningful evaluation of long-run statistics.

Recent findings suggest that the algorithms and computer code have been deposited on GitHub, and the paper and open-source code are accessible online. The researchers hope other teams will build on the modular layer and test it on larger, more complex problems.

In a recent development, the team plans to test progressively larger systems and data-driven models of realistic weather. Realistic-weather performance therefore remains an open research question: the immediate contribution is a formal limit on runaway simulations, while the next tests must establish how that guarantee affects the usefulness of models’ long-term statistics.

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Sources indicate that our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Recent findings suggest that every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures.

According to Meta engineers, modern GPU architectures offer advanced performance-optimization features, including warp specialization, asynchronous memory movement, tensor memory, and cluster-level execution, which depart from Triton's traditional programming model, which simplifies kernel development but abstracts away low-level execution structures.

According to recent reports, for example, a modern FlashAttention kernel may dedicate one warp group to issuing TMA transfers while another executes tensor-core computation. A Blackwell GEMM kernel may coordinate multiple warp groups, TMEM allocations, and cluster resources simultaneously. In both cases, performance depends not only on the computation being performed, but also on how multiple execution agents cooperate.

In a recent development, using these advanced features required "large amounts of architecture-specific orchestration code", as they were not readily available as Triton compilers abstractions. To address this challenge, Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to give engineers explicit control over GPU execution while preserving Triton's programming model.

Sources indicate that TLX introduces a new Multiple Instructions, Multiple Warps (MIMW) execution model that bridges CUDA’s thread-level control and Triton’s block-level abstraction. It extends Triton across five key areas: warp-group orchestration, synchronization, memory orchestration, cluster execution, and optional layout.

Taken together, these capabilities allow TLX to occupy the space between Triton’s productivity and CUDA’s control. Developers retain the advantages of Python, autotuning, and blocked tensor programming while gaining direct access to the execution structures that increasingly determine performance on modern GPUs.

It has been revealed that meta has deployed TLX in production for several months across three major workloads. For GEM model training on thousands of NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, TLX achieved 20–25% end-to-end Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) with up to 2x forward-pass speedup. For In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) in recommendation inference, TLX delivered a 4x speedup on an H100 for a linear compression kernel and reduced compute-intensive net latency up to two-thirds in co-designed models. Finally, in distributed grouped GEMM for LLM pretraining, TLX improved performance, reliability, and maintainability across large GPU fleets for extended training periods.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, AI engineer Kritika Choudary observed:.

When I wrote Flash Attention from scratch in Metal on my M2, the tile loads into threadgroup memory and where to put the barriers were where most of the thinking went, so it's nice to see TLX make that explicit.

On a similar note, Amirul Islam emphasized that:.

In a recent development, making warp-group handoffs explicit while leaving layouts optional feels like a useful boundary. The producer/consumer pipeline is visible in the source, without forcing every fused stage to start with manual layout bookkeeping.

Meta looks to further expand Triton TLX by adding support for additional NVIDIA, AMD, and custom accelerator architectures, automating warp-group orchestration through higher-level abstractions, and integrating TLX with torch.compile.

#46590. Industry News: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Industry News: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one.
  • Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language.
  • Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer aims the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide claims and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Sources indicate that nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one notes, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:.

Recent findings suggest that each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

Recent findings suggest that we trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

It has been revealed that every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and notes why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:.

According to recent reports, "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance.".

The coder reasons about geometry:.

Recent findings suggest that "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart.".

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

Recent findings suggest that what fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

It has been revealed that users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:.

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. An illustration of the same strategy without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

In a recent development, even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

In a recent development, first, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

It has been revealed that we evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a strategy, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

According to recent reports, figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

According to recent reports, palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

Sources indicate that the harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:.
